overview: Mbya Guarani communities maintain connections across parts of Brazil, Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay. Their tekoa combine family relationships, ecological conditions and a shared way of life.

items.text: Seed exchange, experimentation and seasonal planting connect agriculture with community organization.
Extended families cooperate in production, while individual households maintain gardens and share work with relatives.
Families gather materials, make and sell crafts, distributing tasks by age and skill. Objects made for use remain distinct from merchandise.
ISA's early 2000s account describes political intermediaries increasingly taking responsibilities previously combined with spiritual leadership.
Networks between villages persist despite fragmentation by roads, ranches and other land uses. This is a living society, not an extinct kingdom.
